content:
It seems to me that tagging a class (or structure) with the @stacks attribute has no effect. This is rather surprising to me. Is this intentional? MWE

import Mathlib.Tactic.StacksAttribute

/-- info: No tags found. -/
#guard_msgs in
#stacks_tags

@[stacks A04Q] class Foo
@[stacks A04Q] structure Bar

-- issue: expected `Foo` and `Bar` to be tagged
/-- info: No tags found. -/
#guard_msgs in
#stacks_tags

@Damiano Testa did you think about this when writing this attribute?

I did not know this. However, it looks like

attribute [stacks AAAA] Foo
attribute [stacks AAAA] Bar

does add the attribute.
This seems like very surprising behaviour of initialize Lean.registerBuiltinAttribute.
Unless I am doing something wrong, we should probably have a linter that catches uses of attributes that do nothing.
I checked: we have at least a dozen instances of @[stacks] on a structure (demo PR fixing them at #38122), 37 more on a class and 6 kerodon tags on a structure or class. We should have this linter!
(And fix the stacks attribute.)
I've asked about the Lean question: #lean4 > Lean.registerBuiltinAttribute on a structure has no effect
Could you explain what you have in mind for this kind of linter? I'm curious to learn since the implementation isn't immediately obvious to me.

My vague guess: for declaration with an @[attribute] as part of its syntax, check if the declaration in the environment is tagged with that attribute? (This would not complain about

@[stacks AAAA] class Foo
attribute [stacks AAAA] Foo

but hopefully that will be caught during review.) This won't count auto-generated declarations; perhaps this is fine?

I think that Chris is right: attributes may not leave a visible mark in the environment, so it is unclear how the linter could detect that nothing happened when the attribute was applied, since adding nothing could be the intended behaviour!

I wonder if it would make sense to have a "dictionary", where each attribute comes with instructions for the linter to check that it did something (and by default, if nothing is provided, then nothing is checked).
For instance, the stacks attribute modifies an environment extension and this could be what the linter verifies, since the stacks attribute tells it to.
Then the same linter could also lint that every new attribute declaration comes with its dictionary entry... :lol:
This makes sense, but is it overly expensive to double check every addition to environment extensions (for attributes that opt-in to this) as a linter?
I do not know, but every simp call does some attribute lookup, so I imagine that something is fast there.

Also, some attributes already complain when they are not able to do much. Widespread attributes like simp, to_additive, to_dual could be auto-excepted from the check, since they internally perform it anyway.
Anyway, just an idea, maybe it is not worth the trouble.
In that dreamy world where we have periodic CI runs with expensive linters, we could add this linter as well.

I think it could also be implemented as opt-in by the attribute if that helps. For expensive CI linting, we're starting to accumulate more of these at #mathlib4 > Weekly linting log. Maybe this sort of thing could be in scope? (I think we need some better organization of that report though for it be more accessible.)
Running such a check as a weekly linter seems fine: the power of that run is that linters can be too slow to run on every push :-)

Maybe this should be another thread, but I've been thinking a bit about how to make that report easier to work with now that its big enough to be truncated as a Zulip post. It seems it would also help for it to be grouped by the linter it came from, which seems to require wrapping warnings/info in something to attach this information.
More straightforwardly: if this is added as a lint to that report at this moment, it's likely the only place you'd be able to see it is by clicking through to the CI run
Can the PR adding the lint also run it in CI, so we can see how much there is to fix?

For the last weekly lint I added I just built Mathlib locally and mentioned it in the description since I don't have any CI permissions. I think someone who does have permission should be able to trigger from the PR's branch to get the full report.
